title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
How do the conditional independence testing pipeline and significance level affect the connections and highly connected proteins in an estimated protein network?
This project extends a collaborative summer poster by Allison Burnett and Colin Dempsey, supervised by Dr. Daniel Malinsky at SIBDS at Columbia. The summer scripts provide the starting network estimators. The class project adds reproducible comparisons of network size, protein degree, and shared connections, presented in a Quarto website.

How do the conditional independence testing pipeline and significance level affect the connections and highly connected proteins in an estimated protein network?
This project extends a collaborative summer poster by Allison Burnett and Colin Dempsey, supervised by Dr. Daniel Malinsky at SIBDS at Columbia. The summer scripts provide the starting network estimators. The class project adds reproducible comparisons of network size, protein degree, and shared connections, presented in a Quarto website.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
Data and preparation
The dataset attributed to Wang et al. (2016) contains protein measurements from brain tissue. According to the original poster, the samples are from 59 individuals with mild to moderate dementia, with 192 protein variables measured in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The spreadsheet uses identifiers such as Pro1 rather than biological protein names.

The sample ID column is excluded from modeling. All protein measurements are numeric and finite, and no protein column is constant. Protein columns are centered and scaled before fitting. Standardization does not make the variables Gaussian. The dataset contains 11,328 measurements, exceeding the assignment’s minimum of 400.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
Statistical methods
The PC algorithm starts with a fully connected graph. It tests pairs of proteins, first without adjustment and then conditional on other proteins. When the test does not reject independence, the algorithm removes the corresponding connection. It then uses conditional independence information to orient some connections.
The comparison uses six configurations: two testing pipelines at alpha values of 0.01, 0.05, and 0.10.








Pipeline
No conditioning variables
With conditioning variables




Fisher z
Fisher’s z-test
Fisher’s z-test of partial correlation


Pearson + WGCM
Pearson correlation test
WGCM.fix, GAM regression, seven sign weight functions per conditioning variable plus the constant weight



The second pipeline preserves the summer code’s Pearson first step. It is not WGCM at every step: an uncorrelated nonlinear relationship could be removed before a conditional WGCM test is reached. Consequently, these results compare the two complete pipelines and do not isolate the performance of WGCM alone.
For the Gaussian pipeline, zero partial correlation is interpreted as conditional independence under appropriate distributional assumptions, such as joint Gaussianity. WGCM uses weighted residual relationships after regression on the conditioning variables. It can detect some relationships missed by partial correlation, but greater edge counts or higher accuracy are not guaranteed.
A larger alpha generally makes it harder to remove connections. These repeated tests form a graph estimation procedure; alpha is not the whole network’s false discovery rate. PC-stable is used to reduce dependence of the estimated skeleton on variable ordering. Each fit starts with seed 15 and uses the same protein order. WGCM uses 499 simulations for its simulated p-values.
The maximum conditioning set size is 55 in both pipelines, equal to the sample size minus four. This is a numerical upper bound for Fisher’s z-test, not a guarantee that high-dimensional regressions are reliable. With 59 samples, large conditioning sets remain problematic.
For causal interpretation, PC relies on causal Markov, faithfulness, acyclicity, no unmeasured confounding, and suitable conditional independence tests. These assumptions are not verified here. We compare undirected connections: a retained edge does not establish a biological interaction or a causal direction.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
section: Do the same proteins remain highly connected?
text:
Do the same proteins remain highly connected?
The heatmap displays the union of the five highest-degree proteins in each configuration, including ties at the cutoff and excluding proteins with degree zero. The same proteins are displayed for every configuration. Selection here is descriptive and does not test biological importance.
In the heatmaps, F denotes Fisher z and W denotes Pearson + WGCM; the number is alpha.


Code
if (length(selected)) {
  plot_data <- expand.grid(Protein = selected, Setting = settings$Setting,
                           stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  plot_data$Degree <- as.vector(degree_matrix[selected, , drop = FALSE])
  plot_data$Protein <- factor(plot_data$Protein, levels = rev(selected))
  plot_data$Setting <- factor(plot_data$Setting, levels = settings$Setting,
                              labels = settings$Short)
  p_degrees <- ggplot(plot_data, aes(Setting, Protein, fill = Degree)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") + geom_text(aes(label = Degree), size = 3) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F2F5F7", high = "#74B7C5") +
    labs(x = "Pipeline and alpha", y = NULL, title = "Which proteins remain highly connected?")
  print(p_degrees)
  ggsave("results/figures/protein_degrees.png", p_degrees, width = 8,
          height = max(4, 0.23 * length(selected) + 1.5), dpi = 200, limitsize = FALSE)
} else {
  plot.new(); text(0.5, 0.5, "No connections retained at any setting.")
}








Figure 2: Degree of selected highly connected proteins across all six configurations.





The complete degree and rank table, including all proteins, is saved as results/protein_degrees.csv. Rank uses ties rather than arbitrarily assigning different ranks to proteins with equal degree.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
How many connections are shared?
Jaccard similarity is the number of shared connections divided by the number present in either network. A value of 1 means identical edge sets; 0 means no shared connections when at least one network is nonempty. For two empty networks, similarity is marked undefined.


Code
overlap_data <- expand.grid(First = settings$Short, Second = settings$Short,
                            stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
overlap_data$First <- factor(overlap_data$First, levels = settings$Short)
overlap_data$Second <- factor(overlap_data$Second, levels = rev(settings$Short))
overlap_data$Jaccard <- as.vector(overlap)
overlap_data$Label <- ifelse(is.na(overlap_data$Jaccard), "Undefined",
                              sprintf("%.2f", overlap_data$Jaccard))
p_overlap <- ggplot(overlap_data, aes(First, Second, fill = Jaccard)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") + geom_text(aes(label = Label), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F2F5F7", high = "#74B7C5", limits = c(0, 1), na.value = "grey85") +
  coord_equal() + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "How similar are the edge sets?") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
print(p_overlap)
ggsave("results/figures/jaccard_similarity.png", p_overlap, width = 7, height = 6, dpi = 200)








Figure 3: Jaccard similarity of undirected edge sets. F = Fisher z; W = Pearson + WGCM.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
Interpretation and limitations
The results demonstrate substantial sensitivity of estimated protein networks to both the conditional independence testing pipeline and significance level. Across both pipelines, the number of retained connections increased as alpha increased. However, Fisher z consistently produced denser networks than Pearson + WGCM. At alpha = 0.10, Fisher z retained 154 connections, compared with 63 for Pearson + WGCM. The difference was especially pronounced at alpha = 0.01, when the respective networks contained 94 and 1 connection.
The Jaccard similarities further demonstrate differences in the estimated edge sets. Within the Fisher z pipeline, similarity ranged from approximately 0.49 to 0.67 across significance levels. Within Pearson + WGCM, similarity ranged from approximately 0.016 to 0.25. Comparisons between pipelines at matching significance levels also showed relatively low similarity, with Jaccard values of approximately 0.011, 0.108, and 0.247 at alpha values of 0.01, 0.05, and 0.10, respectively. The same-alpha comparison showed that most connections were unique to one pipeline.
The identities of the most highly connected proteins also varied across configurations. Although some proteins, including Pro123, Pro62, Pro159, and Pro82, appeared among the highest-degree proteins in multiple configurations, no single protein consistently dominated all six networks. This suggests that identifying highly connected proteins is also sensitive to analytical choices.
Together, these findings suggest that conclusions about protein connectivity can depend considerably on the selected testing pipeline and significance level. Neither pipeline can be considered more accurate based on these comparisons alone, since the true underlying network is unknown.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
How much do our estimates of protein connections change when we use different statistical tests and significance levels?
During the Summer Institute in Biostatistics and Data Science (SIBDS) at Columbia, Allison Burnett and I worked on estimating networks of proteins under the supervision of Dr. Daniel Malinsky. For this class project, I wanted to take that work a step further: rather than just looking at the networks, I wanted to compare how much they change when we make different statistical choices. I focus on the number of connections, which proteins are most connected, and how many connections the networks share.

During the Summer Institute in Biostatistics and Data Science (SIBDS) at Columbia, Allison Burnett and I worked on estimating networks of proteins under the supervision of Dr. Daniel Malinsky. title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
Data and preparation
The dataset used in our summer project contains measurements of 192 proteins from 59 brain-tissue samples. According to our original poster, the samples came from individuals with mild to moderate dementia, and the measurements were taken from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. The spreadsheet labels the proteins with identifiers such as Pro1, so I refer to them by those identifiers rather than biological names.

I excluded the sample ID column and standardized each protein variable before fitting the networks, so differences in measurement scales would not drive the analysis. Standardizing does not make the data normally distributed. With 59 samples and 192 protein variables, the dataset contains 11,328 protein measurements.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
Statistical methods

How do we estimate a protein network?
I used the PC algorithm, which starts with a possible connection between every pair of proteins. It then uses statistical tests to decide which connections to remove. Some tests look at two proteins directly, while others examine their relationship after accounting for additional proteins. The connections that remain form an estimated network.
The main question for this project is whether those remaining connections depend on which statistical tests we choose.


What are we comparing?
I compared two testing approaches:

Fisher’s z-test: uses correlations (and partial correlations when accounting for other proteins).
Pearson + WGCM: uses a Pearson correlation test when no other proteins are being accounted for, and the Weighted Generalized Covariance Measure (WGCM) for conditional tests. WGCM can capture some relationships that correlation-based tests may miss.

Because the second approach uses Pearson for its first step, this is a comparison of two testing pipelines, not a test of WGCM by itself.
I ran each pipeline at three significance levels: 0.01, 0.05, and 0.10, giving six networks in total. In general, a larger significance level makes it easier for a connection to remain in the estimated network. This gives us a way to see how sensitive the results are to both the test and the threshold we choose.


What should we be careful about?
These are estimated statistical networks, not confirmed biological interactions. Interpreting them causally would require strong assumptions, including no important unmeasured common causes and appropriate conditional independence tests. We cannot verify those assumptions here, especially with only 59 samples and many protein variables. The PC algorithm uses its stable skeleton procedure, and the WGCM tests use simulation-based p-values; additional implementation details are retained in the project code.


No model warnings were recorded during these fits.

section: Do the same proteins remain highly connected?

Do the same proteins remain highly connected?
Next, I wanted to know whether the same proteins would stand out across the six networks. The heatmap includes proteins that ranked among the five most connected in at least one setting (including ties). It shows their number of connections in every setting. A protein appearing here is not necessarily biologically important; it simply has many connections in one or more estimated networks.
In the heatmaps, F means Fisher z, W means Pearson + WGCM, and the number is the significance level.








Figure 2: Degree of selected highly connected proteins across all six configurations.





The full degree and rank results for all proteins are also saved in results/protein_degrees.csv.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
How many connections are shared?
Finally, I compared which specific connections appeared in each network. I used Jaccard similarity: the number of connections two networks share, divided by the number found in either one. A value near 1 means the networks have very similar connections; a value near 0 means they share very few. If both networks have no connections, the value is undefined.

title: How Sensitive Are Estimated Protein Networks?
text:
What did I learn?
The biggest takeaway for me is that the same dataset can produce very different-looking networks depending on the statistical approach. Both pipelines retained more connections as the significance level increased, but Fisher z kept more connections at every level. For example, at 0.10, Fisher z retained 154 connections compared with 63 for Pearson + WGCM. At 0.01, the difference was even more striking: 94 versus 1.
I also wanted to know whether the networks were finding the same connections, even when their sizes differed. The Jaccard comparisons suggest they often were not. At matching significance levels of 0.01, 0.05, and 0.10, the similarities between pipelines were approximately 0.011, 0.108, and 0.247. In other words, the two approaches frequently selected different connections.
The proteins that stood out also changed. Proteins such as Pro123, Pro62, Pro159, and Pro82 appeared among the most connected in multiple settings, but no single protein consistently dominated all six networks.
This matters because a researcher might be tempted to focus on the proteins with the most connections in one estimated network. My results suggest that those conclusions can depend quite a bit on the analysis choices. I can’t say which pipeline is more accurate, because we don’t know the true underlying protein network. What I can say is that comparing methods is important before treating any one network as a definitive picture of the data.
